doc.title: Chuck Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 7, 2023

title: Not imitating Brubeck; the quartet without sax
summary: Lamb never felt pressure to play Dave-style, discusses Mike Demicco in the sax chair, Lucas Pino, and versions of Take Five.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: A killer couple, yeah, in a really good way. Did you feel, especially in the beginning when you were with them, that you should try to give a nod to Dave in the way you played, especially on iconic tunes you know, if you were playing “Blue Rondo a la Turk” or, I mean there are certain things you need to play.
But when it came time to the improvising?

I don’t think so. You know I’m thinking back at the beginning I know for sure you know now and for the last fifteen years, but I don’t think that was ever present. I don’t think I ever felt the need to, you know, I remember at the beginning there’d be some old curmudgeons coming up, “You’ve got some tough shoes to fill young man.” You know that kind of thing. And Dave and I joked about that because I told him that and he said, “Well I’m a 12-1/2, you’re 10-1/2 you know, yeah you do, you’ve got some big shoes — but I never not even close to be intimidated by the chair. I never even thought about it. Because I played the way I played and I know the dude, that’s what Brubeck — wouldn’t want it any other way. You know I’m influenced by him naturally but yeah that’s an interesting, and I’m really grateful for it, that I never felt like oh I’m in a concert and everybody wants to hear Dave-style. It’s like I couldn’t do it for one.

I think it’s interesting that the brothers — I don’t know whose decision this was, but their fourth player is not a saxophone player. Because I think that would have made even this question of trying to sound like Brubeck, even more pressing because then it looks like a real, like we’re trying to re-create —

Right. I think so too. I don’t know, I know Mike Demicco has been playing with those guys, like he was in a band with Dan Brubeck for — he’s been part of the Brubeck thing for 35 years, right? So it was just an organic flow into keeping him. But he has told me, he gets intimidated by — he says, “Yeah man, I know people want to hear saxophone on ‘Take Five.’ They don’t want to hear the guitar.” “Don’t think about it.” Because that sound, even you know we’ve had sax players we’ve played with and do you know Lucas Pino?

That young guy is hot on the scene. Beautiful player. But when Mike can’t be on a gig or something then Lucas or somebody else will. And it really is neat to hear it, you know, I have to admit. How can you not love that sound, the sax with the Brubeck thing.
It’s also interesting to hear different versions of the classic Brubeck “Take Five.”
You know like sometimes if it’s a live version it’s a lot faster and it’s almost like, “No, that’s not how it goes. Didn’t you listen to the record?”
That sounds like a good idea.
Yeah I hear ya. Work on it.
